slides.title: A chat box is the wrong shape for most answers
slides.headline: Ask an agent how sales went this week. The best reply is **three numbers, a chart and a button**, not four paragraphs.
bullets: Generative UI is the layer where an agent's output becomes an interface composed at run time.
The agent still calls a model in a loop; what changes is what the loop emits and what renders it.
The harness codelab built the loop. This series builds what the user sees.
Zero: a page that draws one metric card when the model asks for it.
Hero: the same agent in a browser, a terminal and a host you do not control, on three open formats, with the costs measured.

slides.takeaway: Every step is a directory you can run, with an offline test and a recorded demo.
slides.notes: Start with the problem. Most agent answers are not prose; they are numbers, lists, choices. A chat transcript forces them into paragraphs. Generative UI lets the agent emit an interface. The important framing: the agent loop is unchanged. We only change what it emits and what renders that. That is why this is a companion to the harness codelab rather than a replacement.

slides.notes: This grid is the whole series in one picture. Columns are what the agent emits: static, declarative, open-ended. Rows are where the UI appears: your own product over AG-UI, or a third-party host over MCP Apps. The report's advice is to choose the row first, because it is decided by your product, and then the column, which is a cost and control trade. Point at the cells and name the steps.

slides.title: Static, declarative, open-ended: who decides the layout
bullets: **Static.** Components exist before the model runs. The agent selects one and supplies its props. Lowest cost, safest.
**Declarative.** The agent composes a spec from a catalog: a JSON tree, a flat element map, or a line-oriented language. The renderer walks the spec.
**Open-ended.** No catalog. The model writes HTML, CSS and JavaScript; the host runs it in a sandboxed iframe. Five to ten times the tokens.
**Hybrid.** A catalog with one open-ended component in it. The report's recommended default.
The declarative middle is where the open formats compete: A2UI, OpenUI Lang, json-render.

diagram.rightSub: sandboxed iframe: open-ended only where the catalog does not reach
diagram.caption: The report's diagram: catalog primitives by default

slides.takeaway: Sub-theme 01 builds all four by hand; sub-theme 04 builds the hybrid on OpenUI's reference implementation.
slides.notes: Three modes, one axis. Static is a menu: the agent orders, you cook. Declarative is a kitchen: the agent cooks with your ingredients and your recipes. Open-ended is a blank cheque: anything, at a price, behind glass. The hybrid on the right is the report's answer: keep the catalog as the default and allow one dashed box for the rest.

slides.title: Seven sub-themes, 23 steps, in the order to read them
rows: 01 Foundations
static · declarative tree · open-ended HTML · hybrid
the three modes with no framework, measured in tokens and first paint
02 AG-UI
server · tools and state · from the harness
the transport for your own product: runs, events, state patches, client tools
03 A2UI
by hand · from a model · Lit over AG-UI
Google's protocol: surfaces, flat components, a separate data model, actions
04 OpenUI Lang
parser · React renderer · benchmark · html artifact
the DSL with forward references; the report's token table reproduced; the hybrid on OpenUI's example
05 json-render
catalog · streaming patches · actions and targets
Vercel's element map: one catalog for prompt, validator and registry; one spec, two renderers
06 MCP Apps
an app resource · in a real host · hybrid inside an app
UI inside a host you do not control: a tool result that carries HTML, a bridge, a CSP
07 In the harness
render_ui tool · TrueForge generative UI · hybrid on TrueForge
one agent with two surfaces; a hosted harness's UI language parsed by your own page
slides.caption: Read the sub-themes in order the first time. Each one is self-contained after that.
slides.notes: The roadmap. Foundations first, because every later library is one of those three mechanisms with a package around it. Then the transport, AG-UI. Then the three declarative formats, each in its own sub-theme, with the benchmark in the middle. Then the other transport, MCP Apps. Finally the two harnesses meet the UI layer.

slides.title: Every step has the same shape, in the deck and in the README
bullets: **Theory.** The idea in the report's terms, why it comes now, and a diagram.
**Code walkthrough.** One or two snippets read from the real source at build time, with numbered callouts.
**Recorded result.** The demo output, its real numbers, and the screenshot the demo script took headlessly.
**Checkpoint and takeaway** in the README: one thing to try, one sentence to keep.
Every step directory has an offline test that needs no key, and a Files section that names every file.
slides.takeaway: Numbers on these slides come from recorded runs, never from estimates.
slides.notes: Set expectations for the walkthrough format. Each step is three or four slides: theory, code, result. The code on the slides is extracted from the repository when the deck is built, so it cannot drift from what runs. The numbers are the ones the demo scripts printed. When a step could not run something on the recording machine, the slide says so.

slides.title: What you need to run every step
bullets: Python 3.10 or newer and Node 22. `pip install -r requirements.txt` from the repository root.
A key in `API_KEY`, or `OPENAI_API_KEY=...` in `~/.simple-harness/env`. Every step's `llm.py` reads both; `BASE_URL` and `MODEL` are optional.
`python -m playwright install chromium` once, for the demo screenshots.
Steps with a browser part have a `package.json`; `npm install` there fetches one or two packages. A few steps run one `esbuild` command for a library that ships no browser build.
`python run_tests.py genui` runs every offline test; `python check_snippets.py genui` verifies every README snippet against the code.
